stem: There are 10 targets, 2 of which are down. What does up == 0 return?

options.text: The 2 series for the down targets, each with value 0
options.note: Right. Comparisons filter by default, keeping only matching series with their original values.

options.text: All 10 series, with 1 for down and 0 for up
options.note: That's what up == bool 0 gives.
Comparisons don't count. You'd need count(up == 0) for that.
Series where the comparison is false are dropped.

explanation: Comparison operators filter by default: vector elements for which the comparison is false are dropped. The bool modifier returns 0 or 1 instead.

options.text: Every up series, with value 1 where the target is down and 0 where it's up
options.note: Right. bool turns the filter into a 0/1 result for every matched series.
That's up == 0 without bool.
bool doesn't filter at all.

options.text: The same series with the metric name up preserved
options.note: bool drops the metric name.

explanation: With bool, elements that would have been filtered out get value 0 instead, those that match get 1, and the metric name is dropped.

stem: Which comparison between two scalars is valid?

options.note: Right. Between two scalars, bool must be provided. This returns 1.
Between two scalars the bool modifier is required.
>> isn't a PromQL operator.
bool is a modifier placed after the operator, not a function.

explanation: Between two scalars, the bool modifier must be provided, and these operators return 0 (false) or 1 (true).
hint: There's nothing to filter between two scalars.

stem: What happens to the metric name in (instance_memory_limit_bytes - instance_memory_usage_bytes)?

options.text: It's dropped from the result series
options.note: Right. Any arithmetic binary operation involving vectors drops the metric name.

options.text: The left-hand metric name is kept
options.note: That's true for comparisons without bool, not for arithmetic.
No such merging happens.

options.text: The query fails because the names differ
options.note: Different names are fine. Matching uses labels, not names.

explanation: In any arithmetic binary operation involving vectors, the metric name is dropped.
hint: The result is a new quantity, neither of the originals.

options.text: Divides every series' value by 1024 twice, converting bytes to MiB, with one result per input series
options.note: Right. Between a vector and a scalar, the operator is applied to every sample.

options.text: Returns a single scalar total in MiB
options.note: Scalar arithmetic doesn't aggregate. Every series stays separate.

options.text: Fails, because you can't divide a vector by a scalar
options.note: vector/scalar arithmetic is explicitly supported.
That would be a comparison, not division.

explanation: Between an instant vector and a scalar, the operator is applied to the value of every data sample in the vector.
hint: Think of applying the same division to every row.

stem: Using the data shown, what does method_code:http_errors:rate5m / method:http_requests:rate5m return (with no matching keywords)?

options.note: Right. The left series have method and code labels, the right only method. No label sets match exactly, so nothing pairs.
That needs ignoring(code), plus group_left because there are several codes per method.

options.text: One ratio per method and code
options.note: That needs ignoring(code) group_left.

options.text: An error about different metric names
options.note: Names don't matter for matching. Labels do, and here they don't match.

explanation: By default, two entries match only if they have exactly the same set of labels and values. Unmatched series aren't part of the result.
hint: Compare the label sets on each side.

stem: Which expression returns the fraction of requests with code 500 for each method, using the data shown?

options.note: Right. With code="500" there's one left series per method, and ignoring(code) lets it pair with the right side.
Without ignoring(code) the label sets differ, so nothing matches.
The right side has no code label, so on(code) can't pair series by method.
and is a set operator. It doesn't divide.

explanation: The docs' one-to-one example: ignoring(code) lets errors{method, code="500"} match requests{method}, giving {method="get"} 0.04 and {method="post"} 0.05.
hint: Which label must be left out of the comparison?

stem: How do on(...) and ignoring(...) differ?

options.text: on compares only the listed labels; ignoring compares all labels except the listed ones
options.note: Right. One is a whitelist, the other a blacklist.

options.text: on compares all labels except the listed ones; ignoring compares only the listed ones
options.note: Reversed.
They're opposites in how they choose the labels to compare.

options.text: on is for set operators only; ignoring is for arithmetic only
options.note: Both work with arithmetic, comparison and set operators (and, or, unless).

explanation: on(<label list>) only matches on the provided labels. ignoring(<label list>) ignores the provided labels when matching.
hint: Compare with how by and without behave for aggregation.

stem: In the data shown, each requests series (one per method) must match several errors series (one per method and code). Which modifier makes method_code:http_errors:rate5m / ignoring(code) … method:http_requests:rate5m work?

options.note: Right. The left side has higher cardinality (many-to-one), so you use group_left.
group_right is for when the right side has the higher cardinality.
bool changes comparison output. It doesn't allow many-to-one matching.

options.text: No modifier is needed; ignoring(code) is enough
options.note: Several left series share each right partner, which is many-to-one and must be requested explicitly.

explanation: Many-to-one and one-to-many matching must be explicitly requested with group_left or group_right. left/right names the side with higher cardinality.
hint: Which side has more series per method?

sources.title: Operators › Many-to-one and one-to-many vector matches

stem: What is the result for {method="post", code="404"} in method_code:http_errors:rate5m / ignoring(code) group_left method:http_requests:rate5m, using the data shown?

options.note: That's the post/500 result (6 / 120).
That's the raw error rate before dividing.

options.text: No result, because group_left drops it
options.note: group_left is exactly what lets every code match.

explanation: With group_left, each right-side element matches multiple left elements with the same method. The docs show {method="post", code="404"} 0.175 (21 / 120).
hint: Find the post rows and divide.

sources.title: Operators › Many-to-one and one-to-many vector matches

stem: What does vector1 and vector2 return?

options.text: Elements of vector1 that have an exactly matching label set in vector2, with vector1's values
options.note: Right. and is an intersection that keeps the left-hand values.
That's closer to or.

options.text: Elements of vector1 with no match in vector2
options.note: That's unless.

options.text: The values of vector1 and vector2 added together
options.note: and is a set operation. It doesn't do arithmetic.

explanation: vector1 and vector2 results in the elements of vector1 for which there are elements in vector2 with exactly matching label sets. The metric name and values come from the left side.

stem: Which set operator returns elements of the left vector that have NO matching label set on the right?

options.note: Right. unless is the complement.
and keeps only the elements that do match.
or is a union.
!= compares values. It isn't a set operator.

explanation: vector1 unless vector2 results in the elements of vector1 for which there are no elements in vector2 with exactly matching label sets.
hint: Keep this unless it's also over there.

stem: What does vector1 or vector2 return?

options.text: All elements of vector1, plus elements of vector2 whose label sets don't appear in vector1
options.note: Right. A union where the left side wins on overlap.
That's and.
All of vector1 is included.

options.text: The larger value from each matched pair
options.note: Set operators don't compare values.

explanation: vector1 or vector2 contains all original elements of vector1 and additionally all elements of vector2 that don't have matching label sets in vector1.
hint: Union, with the left side taking priority.

stem: How is 2 * 3 % 2 evaluated, and how is 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 evaluated?

options.note: Right. * and % share a level and are left-associative, while ^ is right-associative.
Same-level operators are left-associative, except ^ which is right-associative.
^ is the exception: it's right-associative.
* and % are left-associative, so * happens first here.

explanation: Operators on the same precedence level are left-associative (2 * 3 % 2 = (2 * 3) % 2), but ^ is right-associative (2 ^ 3 ^ 2 = 2 ^ (3 ^ 2)).
hint: The docs give these exact two examples.

stem: Which operator has the LOWEST precedence?

options.note: Right. or is at the bottom of the precedence list.
and (with unless) sits just above or.
Comparisons are above and, unless and or.
Arithmetic binds more tightly than comparisons and set operators.

explanation: Precedence from highest to lowest: ^; * / % atan2; + -; comparisons; and unless; or.

stem: You want the overall error ratio for a job with many instances. Which approach do the best practices recommend?

options.text: Sum the error rates and the request rates separately, then divide
options.note: Right. Aggregate the numerator and the denominator first, then divide.

options.text: Calculate each instance's ratio, then avg() them
options.note: Averaging ratios isn't statistically valid.

options.text: Take max() of each instance's ratio
options.note: That's the worst instance, not the overall ratio.

options.text: Divide the raw counters without rate()
options.note: Raw counters reflect totals since restart, not current behaviour.

explanation: When aggregating up ratios, aggregate the numerator and denominator separately and then divide. Don't take the average of a ratio or the average of an average.
hint: Instances with very different traffic shouldn't count equally.
